Secure and trusted data sharing in smart 
healthcare using blockchain and IoT integration
Soubhagya Ranjan Mallick1*, Srichandan Sobhanayak2 and Rakesh Kumar Lenkar3
1 Introduction
With the growth in the global population, the number of patients are gradually rising. 
Healthcare organizations are advancing and adopting the latest technologies, which 
alter how this generation is treated. The most exciting technological advancement is 
the Internet of Things (IoT), which connects things and enables them to make deci -
sions independently in intelligent environments. In terms of offering a framework for 
tying together everyday smart devices to collect, share, transmit, and manage data, 
IoT has performed better than the expectations made by researchers during the past 
decades. IoT technology connects heterogeneous healthcare sensor devices to improve 
patient care by minimizing hospital visits [ 1, 2]. Due to the proliferation of IoT medi -
cal devices, healthcare organizations must regularly gather, store, process, and provide 
access to enormous amounts of healthcare data. Centralized storage architecture in 
most IoT healthcare systems can lead to a single point of failure and easy manipulation. 
Discover Internet of Things
Abstract
Remote service delivery and automation using Blockchain and Internet of Things (IoT) 
are revolutionising healthcare operations. Enhancing healthcare data interchange 
and providing real-time treatment is becoming more difficult due to the exponential 
growth of patient populations around the globe. It is still very difficult to develop 
a digital healthcare platform that is entirely decentralised, secure, trustworthy, 
interoperable, and scalable, even if existing studies have improved these platforms 
to improve patient outcomes and reduce hospital visits. This paper proposes a 
robust and scalable healthcare architecture using Blockchain smart contracts and 
IoT, with the integration of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS). By securely storing 
sensitive medical records, the framework enhances data privacy and interoperability 
for patients as well as healthcare professionals. A device proxy monitors potentially 
vulnerable IoT devices and uses cryptography to ensure that data remains private. 
Experimental evaluations of the system’s performance have focused on key factors, 
including healthcare record upload, download, access, and mining times. The results 
show that public healthcare systems based on the Blockchain considerably boost 
efficiency and performance by integrating IPFS.
Keywords Blockchain, IoT, IPFS, Scalability, Smart healthcare, Security, Proxy device

Unfortunately, privacy and security of personal health information are less reliably pro -
tected in IoT healthcare systems [ 3, 4]. Some inexpensive IoT devices used in IoT sys -
tems are very easy targets for malicious nodes. Due to IoT infrastructure storage and 
memory limits, the healthcare system occasionally stops working when a vast volume 
of healthcare data is collected from many linked sensor devices [ 5]. Despite cloud, edge, 
fog, and mist computing systems offering almost endless storage and processing capac -
ity, healthcare data exchanges’ traffic, bandwidth, and processing latency cause the 
network bottleneck. IoT-based healthcare technology faces substantial performance, 
reliability, scalability, interoperability, privacy, trust, decentralization, and security 
challenges [ 6]. Blockchain with IoT integration can help healthcare systems overcome 
centralized communication architecture and cloud-enabled IoT infrastructures. Most 
healthcare organizations adopt Blockchain, a modern digital ledger technology (DLT), to 
solve technical issues when creating IoT healthcare systems. Blockchain’s peer-to-peer 
network performs cryptographically hashed, immutable transactions on a decentral -
ized architecture [ 7, 8]. Blockchain technology allows data transfers without a central 
authority, eliminating a single point of failure in IoT healthcare systems. Due to Block -
chain technology’s distributed computation and decentralized storage, large-scale device 
connectivity, massive data collection, processing, control, communication, storage, and 
analysis are now more feasible than in conventional healthcare systems [ 9, 10]. Block-
chain technology allows doctors, patients, diagnostic centres, and healthcare workers to 
deliver remote patient care, lower treatment costs, and improve patient care. There are 
three distinct types of Blockchains: public, private, and consortium. Blockchains have 
different access mechanisms and verification procedures, which help to strengthen the 
Blockchain-enabled healthcare system. Proof of work is used to verify the creation of 
new blocks in Blockchain technology [ 5, 11]. Ethereum smart contract automatically 
executes healthcare regulations, policies, and the device registration process when large-
scale healthcare devices are connected to the system. The third-party verification pro -
cess is eliminated with this process. With Blockchain-integrated IoT healthcare systems, 
data tampering, malicious activity, and unsecured devices can be easily identified and 
traced. Blockchain-based healthcare solutions simplify the management of current and 
historical medical records through its decentralized nature. Blockchain technology guar-
antees the confidentiality, security, dependability, and integrity of sensitive healthcare 
information [12, 13]. While Blockchain healthcare has several advantages over conven -
tional healthcare systems, the growing complexity of managing an increasing number 
of devices and their associated data makes it more time-consuming to access, process, 
and analyze this information [ 14]. The Interplanetary File System (IPFS), which stores 
data whose hash value is accessible on Blockchain networks, can be used to reduce 
the overload in Blockchain networks. A decentralized, secure, and irreversible health -
care platform has been the primary focus of most earlier research. The Blockchain net -
work has scalability, speed, and security issues when dealing with massive amounts of 
data collected, processed, and stored using large-scale devices. Therefore, IPFS solves 
this problem and makes a scalable healthcare platform. To store the massive amounts 
of healthcare data generated by networked sensor devices, a Blockchain network is 
coupled with the decentralized file-sharing platform IPFS. To obtain the data we need, 
IPFS uses content addressing, which operates on a peer-to-peer network [ 15]. When a 
file is uploaded to IPFS, it is broken down into smaller pieces called chunks, and these

chunks are then distributedly stored with their unique cryptographic hash, known as the 
content identifier (CID), attached to them. CID links all the connected hashes to store 
the root hash, allowing the information chunks to be uniquely identified by their hash 
values. An open network like BitTorrent allows for the movement of files. In IPFS, the 
addresses of stored data are maintained in a DHT. IPFS uses a Merkle Tree structure to 
store the hash values of linked files. To improve healthcare systems’ speed, accessibility, 
storage capacity, and scalability, blockchain networks only save the file address rather 
than the entire file. The Blockchain network within healthcare organizations are linked 
to the IPFS similarly to how webpages are linked. IPFS keeps a local hash file for fre -
quently viewed files and enables rapid access to these files on subsequent tries. Anyone 
accessing the hash address can download a file via the IPFS distributed network [ 16]. In 
IPFS, once a file is uploaded, its hash is shared among all peer nodes in the network for 
instant access and to prevent data from having a single point of failure. Here, scalability, 
interoperability, and consistency issues are addressed with the IPFS, which also offers 
security and boosts the efficiency of healthcare systems.
1.1 Motivation
Although we cannot entirely eradicate every disease that affects people today, we can 
adopt innovative technology to reduce the severity of patients’ conditions and offer 
superior healthcare for a healthier world. Most past research focused on sensor-based 
healthcare systems to deliver remote healthcare services, improve patient cure rates, 
and eliminate the need for patients to travel to healthcare facilities. Still, the system’s 
privacy, scalability, security, and efficiency should have been addressed. In recent years, 
healthcare organizations have explored Blockchain integration with IoT to enable all IoT 
devices to interact without relying on trustworthy third parties. Blockchain technology 
has enabled healthcare businesses to effectively manage a growing number of distributed 
data transactions instead of traditional centralized ones. As more patients are added, the 
Blockchain healthcare system’s ability to connect, store, preserve, transact, and retrieve 
data becomes more challenging. This is because the system saves data in the Blockchain 
network. This framework integrates an IPFS with the Blockchain network to address the 
challenges of scalability, interoperability, efficiency, and security and improve storage 
capability.
1.2 Novel contributions
1. It presents a Blockchain-based novel framework to address healthcare systems’ data 
privacy, security, interoperability, scalability, and efficiency challenges.
2. It Integrates an Interplanetary File System (IPFS) with the Blockchain network to 
reduce blockchain network overload and enhance healthcare systems’ scalability and 
storage capacity.
3. It employs a device proxy to keep track of vulnerable devices and a cryptographic 
message authentication mechanism to keep data confidential.
1.3 The article structure
This paper’s remaining sections are organized as follows: Sect.  2 reviews the blockchain 
healthcare related works. The system model of the M-Blockchain framework is pre -
sented in Sect.  3. The proposed model’s implementation is described in Sect.  4, whereas

2 Related works
This section presents the literature on the opportunities and challenges of implement -
ing technological advancements in Smart healthcare systems. Some of the best research 
works published in medical fields are highlighted here.
Zheng et al. [17] proposed an IPFS-based Blockchain system to reduce the data storage 
in Blockchain networks and increase processing speed. They implemented this scheme 
on the Bitcoin Blockchain. A zigzag-based novel storage model is proposed by Chen et 
al. [18] to increase the block storage model. High throughput is achieved in this model 
with the implementation of IPFS. Pan et al. [ 19] proposed an edge-IoT framework, 
EdgeChain, based on Blockchain and smart contracts for secure and scalable commu -
nication. Jolfaei et al. [ 9] discuss different system models and how to improve the scal -
ability of Blockchain-based systems. Off-chain and on-chain-based models can be used 
to overcome the scalability issues in Blockchain-based IoMT systems. Providing a clear 
route for tracing the activities and achieving a high level of trustworthiness, Nyaletey 
et al. [20] proposed block IPFS a Blockchain-enabled IPFS. For secure storage, safe data 
sharing, and maintaining security while working in the system, Li et al. [ 21] proposed a 
hyperledger fabric and Interplanetary File System to safely share healthcare information. 
On-chain and off-chain Blockchain-based Interplanetary File system solves scalability, 
confidentiality, and storage problems. This model increases the confidentiality of shar -
ing healthcare information proposed by Mani et al. [ 22]. A Blockchain-based Interplan -
etary File System is proposed by Mamun et al. [ 23] for implementing Blockchain EMR 
and providing access rules. An immutable Blockchain-based Interplanetary File System 
is proposed by Sultana et al. [ 24] for enhancing the security of healthcare data transac -
tions. For easy access, consistency, integrity, availability, and security, Kumar et al. [ 25] 
proposed off-chain data storage. Interplanetary File System uses blockchain technology 
in its model. Alrebdi et al. [ 26] proposed a Blockchain smart contract-based decentral -
ized medical record system with several features: immutability, anonymity, security, 
decentralized, and tamper-proof. Interplanetary File Systems and cloud computing 
technology are used here for medical record-keeping. A security and privacy protection 
scheme using Blockchain technology is proposed by Tan et al. [ 27] with traceable and 
direct revocation for COVID-19 records. Cipher text policy attribute-based encryption 
is used here. Distributed patient-centric image management (PCIM) system, an Ethe -
reum Blockchain, and an Interplanetary File System (IPFS) are proposed by Jabarulla 
et al. [ 28] for decentralized storage and global access to medical images. A systematic 
review of Blockchain-based PHRs has been done by Fang et al. [ 11] for limitations, 
design choices, and future direction. The attribute-based encryption scheme is proposed 
by Sun et al. [ 29] for the storage and sharing of medical records using Blockchain tech -
nology and the Interplanetary File System.

3 System model
Processing real-time healthcare data, timely patient monitoring, and providing health -
care services are challenging for healthcare providers worldwide [ 30, 31]. Although 
most existing Blockchain-integrated IoT systems provide smart healthcare systems, as 
the number of connected healthcare devices grows, the system’s access to, processing, 
and storage of healthcare data slows down. The inability to deliver continuous, real-time 
patient care is a major concern for many healthcare facilities. Patients may get worse 
or possibly die if they do not receive the best possible care immediately. To address 
the shortcomings of current Blockchain-integrated IoT healthcare systems, we have 
proposed an IPFS-integrated Blockchain-IoT healthcare system. Figure  1. depicts the 
proposed framework, which is secure, interoperable, and scalable for healthcare organi -
zations. It integrates Blockchain, IoT, and IPFS (Table 1).
3.1 Framework description
In this system, real-time patient care is prioritized above all else. Still, strong privacy, 
security, and scalability solutions for accessing, processing, transferring, and storing 
healthcare data are also paramount. Each “block" in the Blockchain healthcare system 
is a timestamped, cryptographically linked, distributed, and immutable set of records. 
The proposed system employs smart contracts built on the Ethereum platform to check 
if IoT devices adhere to pre-defined privacy policies and other limitations. Device access 
permissions are granted to devices via a smart contract-defined access management 
and authentication method. All healthcare IoT devices used in this framework fall into 
secured and unsecured categories. Unsecured IoT devices are cheap and vulnerable 
and cannot execute privacy policies and agreements. These devices are connected via 
a device proxy. The device proxy authorises these gadgets to the system and monitors 
their behaviour. The proposed framework also uses decentralized and cryptographically

3.2 Encryption and decryption process
The two-stage process of encryption and decryption is depicted in Fig.  4. This frame -
work hashes User1’s source text into a message digest. Message digests are in an unread-
able format. The source text and the sender’s private key are used to construct a digital 
signature through encryption and hashing. The original encrypted text, the message 
digest, and the digital signature are sent onto the Blockchain. The receiver (user 2) sepa -
rates the source text and the encrypted message digest. Using User1’s public key, decrypt 
the encrypted message digest and extract the message digest. The message digest is com-
puted from the original text using the same hashing technique. After computing mes -
sage digests, they are compared with one another. If the digests of the two messages are 
the same, then the data has not been tampered with, and if they are different, then the 
message has been tampered with.

4 Implementation
4.1 Environmental setup
The proposed healthcare system was implemented in the IoT and cloud computing lab 
at IIIT Bhubaneswar with the system configuration of Intel Core i7-1165G7, 4.70 GHz 
processor, with a cache memory of 12 MB, running Windows 10 Professional on a 1 
terabyte (TB) hard drive with a 512 gigabyte (GB) solid-state drive (SSD) and a 64-bit 
operating system. All machines are connected to the same private network for experi -
mental evaluation. One machine is the master machine, and the others are the client 
machines. Different data sizes, including 20MB, 40MB, 60MB, 80MB, 100MB, 120MB, 
and 140MB, are chosen to evaluate the performance of the proposed model. Table 2 lists 
the software, frameworks, and tools used in the proposed framework.
4.2 Execution process
Three algorithms have been presented for this proposed framework. Algorithm 1 shows 
the registration and uploading of the file into the proposed framework. The smart con -
tract checks device authentication when users register for the decentralized application.

4.3 Proof of the correctness of algorithms
The use of cryptographically bound, non-transferable identification tokens, as illustrated 
in Algorithm 1, is integral to the system. The registration process incorporates protec -
tions to ensure the security of personal information while confirming identity. No one 
can deny or alter a registered identity because of the immutability of the blockchain. 
Consistent enforcement of registration rules across all participants is ensured by smart 
contracts. Each user is able to access the precise data that was initially uploaded, as 
shown in Algorithm 2. The data is protected so that only authorised people can access it. 
The integrity of the obtained data is confirmed by comparing it with IPFS hashes. Addi -
tionally, this algorithm completes its execution in a finite number of steps. Deciphering 
the ciphertext with the right parameters and key returns the original plaintext, as dem -
onstrated in Algorithm 3. Hash functions on the Blockchain and IPFS CID ensure that 
data remains secure during storage and transaction.
5 Result analysis
We have conducted a number of experiments on various machines in the same network 
to evaluate the performance of our proposed framework. Using content-addressed hash-
ing, the platform facilitates efficient distributed healthcare data storage, access, and 
retrieval. This architecture is user-friendly and effective at preserving the confidential -
ity, availability, and integrity of sensitive healthcare information. We employed seven 
distinct healthcare file sizes across multiple machines to test the proposed framework. 
Tests of the framework’s performance were conducted using the metrics of upload, 
download, access, and mining times.
  – Upload Time: Upload time is the time a node takes to upload new transactions to the 
Blockchain network. Upload time depends on network speed and node processing 
power.
  – Download Time: Blockchain download time is the time it takes a node to download 
the file and synchronize with the whole network. Blockchain size, network speed, 
and node processing power determine download time.
  – Access Time: Blockchain access time is the time it takes a user to access a transaction 
or block. It varies depending on the Blockchain’s size and the user’s device’s 
computational power.
  – Mining Time:  Blockchain mining time is the time it takes miners to solve 
cryptographic puzzles and add new blocks or transactions. Puzzle difficulty and 
miner node processing speed affect mining time. Network protocol determines block 
time, which differs from each Blockchain.
We’ve considered healthcare files of varying sizes, uploaded them from several machines, 
and timed how long each file took to be added to Blockchain and IPFS. Figure 5. displays 
the difference in upload speed between IPFS and Blockchain. Observation indicates that 
the time required to upload files to the Blockchain network increases with file size. The 
graph in Fig.  5. indicates that IPFS uploads faster than Blockchain. The time it takes to 
upload a file to the IPFS network grows as the file size increases; however, after a certain 
file size, it increases minimally, much faster than uploading to Blockchain. Figure 6. com-
pares Blockchain and IPFS download timings. This graph depicts the experimental mod-
el’s results, which show that downloading the file through Blockchain takes noticeably
